title: Real-time multilingual ASR: route between small models
text:
Real-time speech recognition struggles with language switches. After a switch, models tend to produce gibberish until they register the new language, translate instead of transcribing, or drop whole passages. The usual fix is a bigger multilingual model, but every added language pushes it further out of reach of CPU-only deployments.
This is a small proof of concept that goes the other way: route between small monolingual streaming models and let a coordinator deal with the switches. Code: realtime-multilingual-asr-router.
Demo video: watch the walkthrough, with the live demo at 3:10.

title: Real-time multilingual ASR: route between small models
text:
Architecture
Three open-source pieces, all lightweight and built to run on edge devices:

Streaming ASR: Zipformer transducers of about 100M parameters each. The models come from KrokoAI for en/fr/es/de/it/pt/nl, plus a Vosk-based model for Russian, all run through sherpa-onnx.
VAD: Silero, to find speech boundaries.
Language ID (LID): SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN (VoxLingua107), also small and CPU-friendly.

Because every component is that light, this is a way to get multilingual real-time transcription on edge hardware, with no GPU and no large model to fit in memory.
The coordinator keeps the audio buffered, watches boundaries, and can re-run a segment when the language changes.



Architecture of the router: streaming ASR models, VAD, language ID and the coordinator that keeps the audio buffered.

title: Real-time multilingual ASR: route between small models
text:
Rollback

Audio goes straight to the current ASR model. We never wait for language ID before showing text.
In the background, LID runs on growing windows of audio since the last VAD boundary.
If the detected language differs from the current one and confidence crosses a threshold, swap the ASR model, roll back to the last VAD boundary, and re-infer the buffered audio.
After a set duration of silence, emit a final, always produced by the right model.

The price is a few wrong-language partials that get replaced within moments. Finals have clean language boundaries. Rollback is cheap because the models are tiny and the buffer never spans more than one segment.

The table shows word error rate in percent, so lower is better. Deepgram and ElevenLabs are mature production cloud APIs. The only open alternative I compared against is Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime, which has about 40 times more parameters than the models used here.

On monolingual speech, ElevenLabs and Voxtral are stronger and Deepgram is on par, which is what to expect from models of about 100M parameters. On switches between utterances, the router is ahead of every system tested, because it transcribes each side with its own specialist model and re-runs a segment as soon as the language changes.



Word error rate on code-switching test sets for the router and the compared systems.

title: Real-time multilingual ASR: route between small models
text:
Where it breaks
Language switches inside a sentence, like Spanglish, happen faster than the VAD can find a boundary. Rollback rarely fires, so the wrong model is often used, which explains the 41% above. That is still far ahead of the open alternative, Voxtral, at 76%, even if the cloud APIs do better. I think these cases need their own specialized models, one for Spanglish, one for Singlish, and so on, rather than a smarter router.

title: Real-time multilingual ASR: route between small models
text:
Scaling to more languages
Adding a language only means dropping in another public model. Any online transducer supported by sherpa-onnx works, so the approach can cover many languages without growing any single model or its per-stream CPU cost.
